findings.headline: Sports income is budgeted at (418,000) by 2029/30, from nil in 2026/27, reducing its net cost from £792,984 to £374,984.
findings.detail: The Sports line has no income in 2026/27 but builds to (42,000) in 2027/28, (230,000) in 2028/29 and (418,000) in 2029/30. Expenditure stays flat at £792,984, so the net cost falls in each year.
findings.matters: A leisure service moving from full subsidy to a planned income surplus is a specific income-generation plan that other councils running leisure contracts will want to compare.

findings.headline: Commercial Sites income is budgeted to rise from (10,657,839) in 2026/27 to (11,820,662) in 2029/30, with net income from (9,094,248) to (10,257,071).
findings.detail: Income from commercial sites increases in each year of the plan, while the expenditure budget is held flat at £1,563,591. The increase is therefore shown entirely in the net income figure.
findings.matters: Commercial property income is a rental stream that lenders and finance directors track closely, and a plan that relies on it rising every year is a test of whether that growth is delivered.

findings.headline: Parking Services - Off Street income is budgeted at (10,039,647) from 2027/28, down from (10,593,647) in 2026/27.
findings.detail: The off-street parking income budget falls by £554,000 from 2027/28 and then stays at that level through 2029/30. Expenditure is unchanged, so the net budget for off-street parking moves from (6,562,484) to (6,008,484).
findings.matters: A lower parking income assumption that holds for the rest of the plan is a direct test of the council's car park revenue, which other councils with similar assets will compare.

findings.headline: Inflation Contingency Provisions rise from £700,637 in 2026/27 to £6,033,527 in 2029/30.
findings.detail: The inflation contingency is the largest single driver of the increase in Corporate Management's net budget in the paper. It grows in each year, from £3,428,637 in 2027/28 to £4,731,872 in 2028/29, with no income offset.
findings.matters: A contingency growing almost nine-fold over the plan period shows how much of the future budget the council is holding against inflation rather than allocating to services.

findings.headline: The 'Contributions to/from Reserves' line shows (404,400) of reserve income from 2027/28, a net (374,612) in each year to 2029/30.
findings.detail: In 2026/27 the reserves line is a small net contribution of £25,388. From 2027/28 the income side shows (404,400) and the net line shows (374,612) in each following year, so the budget relies on reserves in each year of the plan.
findings.matters: A budget that draws on reserves in every year of the plan, rather than in a one-off, shows how far the council depends on reserves to balance its revenue position.
findings.figures: Reserve income: (£404,400) per year from 2027/28; net: (£374,612) per year from 2027/28; 2026/27 net: £25,388

findings.headline: Interest & Financing Costs rise from a gross £13,010,986 in 2026/27 to £14,377,281 in 2029/30, and from a net £5,032,208 to £6,398,503.
findings.detail: The gross expenditure budget for interest and financing steps up in 2028/29 and again in 2029/30, while the income budget of (7,978,778) is held flat across all four years. The net budget is therefore higher in each year of the plan.
findings.matters: A rising net financing budget with unchanged income is a direct measure of the council's cost of borrowing, which other councils and lenders compare directly.

findings.headline: The plan shows a 'Balance of savings to find' of £517,300 in 2029/30 and £58,465 in 2028/29, with nil in 2026/27 and 2027/28.
findings.detail: The grant funding and savings block closes with a 'Balance of savings to find' row. The paper shows the balance as nil until 2028/29, then (58,465) in 2028/29 and (517,300) in 2029/30. The paper does not say here how that balance is to be met.
findings.matters: A finance director or lender will want to know whether the unfound savings in the later years have a named solution, since the amount rises from nil to £517,300 in the final year of the plan.

findings.headline: The 2026/27 outturn identified no issues that would affect the 2027/28 budget, and the year-end position is due to Cabinet in December.
findings.detail: The paper says no issues were identified that were not already included in the budget assumptions. It states that the forecast year-end position will be reported to Cabinet in December.
findings.matters: A clean outturn read-across to the next budget is a signal that finance directors and lenders look for when assessing forecasting accuracy.
findings.quote: There were no issues identified that would impact the 2027/28 budget which had not already been included within the budget assumptions.

findings.headline: A multi-year settlement was announced after the fair funding review, covering three years from 2026.
findings.detail: The paper says the fair funding review was implemented in April 2026 with updated Relative Needs Formulas and a full reset of business rates baselines. It says the multi-year settlement provides more stability over three years.
findings.matters: A three-year settlement after a full funding reset is a planning horizon that finance directors and lenders across local government will be assessing.
findings.quote: The multi-year settlement was also announced, providing more stability over a three year period.

findings.headline: Council tax value collected after April and over the following five years is expected to meet or exceed budgeted amounts.
findings.detail: The paper says the in-year collection rate is expected to be slightly below target for the current year. It also says the council tax support changes agreed in January 2026 are expected to help the collection rate.
findings.matters: Long-run collection performance is a core input to council tax income, and a clear recovery expectation is useful for benchmarking against other councils' collection trends.
findings.figures: £14.6m council tax budget; 9,891 residents receiving council tax support
findings.quote: the value collected after April and over the following 5 years is expected to meet or exceed the amounts budgeted for:

findings.headline: Commercial rents are budgeted at £12m for 2027/28 and are at budgeted levels, while downward pressure on high street rents continues.
findings.detail: The paper says rental income makes up a significant proportion of the council's income, so shortfalls would affect future services. It also says the council needs to replenish the commercial rent stabilisation reserve.
findings.matters: Commercial property income is a large share of revenue at many councils, and high street rent pressure is a common exposure that peers and lenders monitor.
findings.figures: £12m commercial rents in 2027/28
findings.quote: Rents continue to be impacted by the economic climate but are at budgeted levels.

findings.headline: Further savings are expected to be required in 2028/29, after 2027/28 savings from increased fees and charges and minor efficiencies.
findings.detail: The paper says there is huge uncertainty over the budget because of the economic position and the lack of clarity over local government reorganisation. It describes the 2027/28 savings as a combination of fees, charges and minor efficiencies.
findings.matters: A forward savings requirement with no named proposals yet is the kind of gap a finance director at a peer council will compare against their own medium-term plan.
findings.quote: There will likely be further savings required in 2028/29.

findings.headline: Planned capital expenditure is outstripping capital receipts, which the paper says will increase borrowing and revenue costs.
findings.detail: The paper says further revenue savings will be needed unless further revenue contributions close the funding gap or projects become self-funding. It also says the value and timing of capital receipts is subject to significant uncertainty.
findings.matters: A gap between capital spend and receipts converts directly into borrowing and revenue cost, which bears on any council with a disposals-funded programme.
findings.quote: As for previous years, planned capital expenditure is outstripping receipts, which will lead to increased borrowing and revenue costs, requiring further revenue savings to ensure a balanced budget

findings.headline: Short-term borrowing from other local authorities is being used to reduce borrowing costs, with interest rate rises identified as an in-year risk.
findings.detail: The paper says this approach comes at a risk that borrowing costs will rise in year if interest rates increase. It also notes that loans are generally taken out on a fixed-rate basis for certainty.
findings.matters: Reliance on short-term local authority funding is a specific choice whose exposure to rate movements other councils and lenders will want to compare.
findings.quote: Short-term borrowing from other local authorities is also being used to reduce borrowing costs, though this comes at a risk that if interest rates increase, borrowing costs will rise in year.

findings.headline: Borrowing costs are budgeted at £13.3m for 2027/28, and external borrowing will increase as internal borrowing reduces.
findings.detail: The paper says internal borrowing will fall as reserves are used, so external borrowing will need to increase. The MRP is already in the budget, so the additional cost is interest only.
findings.matters: Falling internal borrowing and rising external borrowing shift the council towards new market funding, which lenders and finance directors track closely.
findings.figures: £13.3m borrowing costs in 2027/28
findings.quote: This means that external borrowing will need to increase.

findings.headline: The council expects business rates growth in 2027/28, after the business rates reset placed it in a safety net threshold that triggered a government top-up.
findings.detail: The paper says the top-up payment has reduced for 2027/28. It also says the council is now expecting to achieve business rates growth, which is budgeted at £0.2m.
findings.matters: The move from safety-net top-up to expected growth is a direct change in business rates income that other councils after the 2026 reset will recognise.
findings.figures: £0.2m business rates growth; £5.6m business rates baseline; £6.0m formula grant including business rates
findings.quote: the council are now expecting to achieve business rates growth.

findings.headline: £0.4m is expected to be drawn from reserves in 2027/28 to balance the budget, and the general fund minimum balance is assumed to be 10% or £3m.
findings.detail: The paper says reserves are being reviewed so that contributions can be reinstated when possible. It states that low reserves make it difficult to manage unforeseen impacts, so the minimum balance is set to rebuild resilience.
findings.matters: A finance director at another council would compare the drawdown and the minimum-balance target against their own reserve position and rebuild plans.
findings.figures: £0.4m drawn from reserves in 2027/28; GF minimum balance 10% or £3m
findings.quote: Around £0.4m is expected to be drawn from reserves in 2027/28 to balance the budget in that year.

findings.headline: The 2027/28 estimate for repairs and maintenance is £11,089,660, up from a forecast £9,244,019 in 2026/27.
findings.detail: Repairs and maintenance is forecast at £9,244,019 for 2026/27, below the original budget of £9,535,567. The 2027/28 estimate rises above both figures.
findings.matters: Repairs spending is one of the largest HRA costs, so a rise of this size in the next year's estimate is a pressure a finance director would plan for.

findings.headline: Forecast 2026/27 interest payable is £433,000 against £726,000 in the original budget, while external borrowing repayments are forecast at £382,640 against £89,640.
findings.detail: The two lines move in opposite directions by the same amount between the original and forecast columns. The paper does not give a reason for either change.
findings.matters: A shift of this size between interest and principal repayments points to a change in the borrowing position, which a lender would want explained.
findings.figures: Interest payable: £726,000 original 2026/27, £433,000 forecast 2026/27; External borrowing repayments: £89,640 original 2026/27, £382,640 forecast 2026/27
findings.quote: 260,373 Interest payable (item 8 debit) 726,000 433,000 261,000

findings.headline: The 2026/27 original budget opened with a £4,683,114 HRA balance, against £16,470,984 shown as the 31 March 2026 position.
findings.detail: The original 2026/27 column shows the balance as at 1 April at (4,683,114), while the actual column shows the balance at 31 March 2026 at (16,470,984). The paper does not explain the difference between the two figures.
findings.matters: A budget set on an opening balance well below the outturn shown in the same paper is worth comparing with how other councils set their opening reserve assumptions.
findings.figures: £4,683,114 original 2026/27 opening balance; £16,470,984 actual balance at 31 March 2026

findings.headline: The 2026/27 forecast includes a £12,000,000 transfer to the Major Repairs Reserve, taking the HRA balance from £16,470,984 to £5,286,881.
findings.detail: The transfer appears only in the forecast 2026/27 column, with the original 2026/27 budget showing £6,450,000 as the annual transfer to the Major Repairs Reserve. The paper does not state what the transfer is for in the text shown.
findings.matters: A balance falling from £16.5m to £5.3m in one year is a reserve drawdown that a lender and peer finance officers would check against the capital programme.
findings.figures: £12,000,000 transfer to Major Repairs Reserve (forecast 2026/27); £16,470,984 forecast opening balance; £5,286,881 forecast closing balance
findings.quote: 0 Transfer to Major Repairs Reserve 0 12,000,000 0

findings.headline: The HRA recorded an £8,170,956 surplus in 2025/26, and its balance rose from £8,300,028 to £16,470,984 over the year.
findings.detail: The actual 2025/26 column shows a deficit/(surplus) for the year of (8,170,956), with no transfer to the Major Repairs Reserve in that year. The balance at 31 March 2026 is shown as (16,470,984).
findings.matters: The 2025/26 reserve build is the opening position for the 2026/27 movements that follow, so a finance officer comparing peers would want to see it.
findings.figures: £8,170,956 surplus (2025/26 actual); £8,300,028 balance at 1 April 2025; £16,470,984 balance at 31 March 2026

findings.headline: Band D council tax increases are shown as 2.99%, 2.97%, 2.99% and 2.90% across 2026/27 to 2029/30.
findings.detail: The Band D equivalent rises from £254.43 in 2026/27 to £277.65 in 2029/30, with annual increases of £7.38, £7.56, £7.83 and £7.83. The paper does not state whether these rises include any adult social care precept.
findings.matters: The council tax rise is a major source of the income that funds the net budget, so a reader comparing councils can benchmark it against their own increase.

findings.headline: Capital Financing & Interest is £13,445k in 2028/29 and £600k in 2029/30.
findings.detail: The line is £12,779k in 2026/27 and £12,845k in 2027/28 before falling sharply in 2029/30. The paper does not give the reason for the fall in this summary table.
findings.matters: Capital financing costs of this size bear on the council's borrowing position, so a reader would want the explanation for a fall of this scale before relying on the figure.
findings.quote: Capital Financing & Interest 12,779 12,845 13,445 600

findings.headline: The contribution from reserves is £25k in 2026/27 and £375k in each of 2027/28, 2028/29 and 2029/30, with the later years shown in brackets.
findings.detail: The paper's reserves line changes sign between 2026/27 and the following years. The summary table does not explain the direction of the flows in the brackets.
findings.matters: A finance officer would want to know whether the council is drawing on reserves or adding to them across the plan, since the answer changes the sustainability of the budget.
findings.quote: Contribution from reserves 25 (375) (375) (375)

findings.headline: A Balance of Savings line of £58k in 2028/29 and £517k in 2029/30 is shown in brackets in the net budget, with nil in the two earlier years.
findings.detail: The paper records no balance of savings in 2026/27 or 2027/28. The entries in brackets in 2028/29 and 2029/30 are the only savings figures shown in the summary table, and the paper gives no narrative on them here.
findings.matters: A savings line that rises from nil to £517k within the plan is a delivery target the council will need to hit, and a reader can check it against the savings plan in the wider paper.
findings.figures: Balance of Savings £0k, £0k, £(58)k, £(517)k for 2026/27 to 2029/30
findings.quote: Balance of Savings 0 0 (58) (517)

findings.headline: The net budget rises from £25,864k in 2026/27 to £29,764k in 2029/30.
findings.detail: The paper's net budget line increases in each year of the plan. The council tax requirement rises from £14,170k to £16,053k over the same period, while grant income total moves from £(11,694)k to £(13,711)k.
findings.matters: A finance director, here or at a peer council, can compare how much the net budget grows against grant and council tax income growth over the same four years.

findings.headline: New Waste Depot Relocation contingency of £500,000 is added in 2027/28
findings.detail: The paper adds a new contingency line for the waste depot relocation in 2027/28. The appendix does not say what the relocation will cost in total or where the contingency sits against the main scheme.
findings.matters: A new contingency for a depot relocation signals an expected cost overrun or unresolved cost risk that other councils would want to compare.
findings.quote: NEW Waste Depot Relocation contingency 0 0 500,000 500,000 0 0 0 0

findings.headline: Kings Hall building improvements are budgeted at £934,345 in 2026/27 and £1,500,000 in 2027/28
findings.detail: The Kings Hall line is one of the larger building schemes in the 2026/27 and 2027/28 years and has no entries after 2027/28. The paper does not state the funding source for this line.
findings.matters: A finance director would want to know how a building scheme of this size is funded and whether the 2027/28 figure is committed.
findings.quote: AC2620 Kings Hall building improvements 934,345 934,345 1,500,000 1,500,000 0 0 0 0

findings.headline: Park and Ride option is shown at £8,000,000 in the 2028/29 column, after £1,500,000 in 2027/28 and £500,000 in 2026/27
findings.detail: The Park and Ride option is the largest single line in the plan for the later years. The paper lists it as an option, not a committed scheme, so the £8,000,000 sits in the forward programme without a confirmed funding decision in this appendix.
findings.matters: A single £8m option falling in one year is a concentrated borrowing or grant requirement that other councils and lenders would want to track.

findings.headline: General Fund capital programme has a revised 2026/27 budget of £12,914,067, £7,794,594 for 2027/28, £10,069,875 for 2028/29 and £2,070,621 for 2029/30
findings.detail: The totals row gives 2026/27 expenditure of £13,004,067 less £60,000 income, and 2027/28 expenditure of £7,865,594 less £71,000 income. The 2028/29 original budget is £10,069,875 and the 2029/30 original budget is £2,070,621. The programme is front-loaded into 2026/27 and 2028/29, with a sharp drop in between.
findings.matters: A finance director can compare the shape of this programme with their own borrowing profile, and a lender can see when the General Fund's capital spending and any borrowing need are expected to peak.

findings.headline: Recruitment and retention of professionally qualified housing staff is described as "challenging" in all fields.
findings.detail: The paper says experienced staff are needed to implement the service improvement plan and the Conduct and Competency Standard, and the draft budget increases capacity in the areas where weaknesses are identified. The council competes with other councils, registered providers and the private sector for these skills.
findings.matters: Staffing capacity tied to a regulatory improvement plan is a people cost and delivery risk other councils with similar regulatory findings will recognise.

findings.quote: However, recruitment and retention of professionally qualified and experienced staff is challenging in all fields

findings.paper_title: Draft Housing Revenue and Capital Budget 2027/28 & App 1 and 2 Non key
findings.headline: The 2027/28 HRA revenue budget covers one year only, with no projections for following years.
findings.detail: The paper says the revenue budget is for one year only because many elements need constant review. It also says the HRA Business Plan 2019 is being refreshed from November 2026 to reflect the regulatory findings and the investment programme.
findings.matters: A single-year revenue budget with a business plan refresh underway means the multi-year HRA position is not yet set out, which lenders and peers will want to see when it is published.

findings.headline: Sheltered Plus service charges were reduced on 14 September 2026 after reconfiguration, and the paper says the HRA no longer needs a large subsidy for those schemes.
findings.detail: The Older Persons' Accommodation Working Group review was adopted on 19 January 2026, and services in the four former Sheltered Plus schemes have been reconfigured to the independent living model. Work is underway to install modern CCTV and door entry equipment.

findings.headline: In 2026/27 the council identified seven homes to buy for the HRA, partly funded by the Local Authority Housing Fund Round 4.
findings.detail: The paper separately notes that 20 homes are being acquired for the General Fund as temporary accommodation, with that project still being analysed before further funding is proposed.
findings.matters: Acquisitions funded partly by a government housing fund add to the HRA stock and depend on external grant, which other councils also rely on.

findings.headline: The draft budget contains £3.5 million to develop HRA sites at East Street and Warwick Road and to progress pipeline projects to the planning stage.
findings.detail: The paper says the council's own land sites are small and constrained, and that buying homes direct from developers and securing s.106 housing is the most cost-effective route to scale. Commercial discussions are described as being at an early stage and subject to location, valuation, mix and viability.
findings.matters: Development funding from the HRA for new council homes is a capital commitment that peer councils with similar small sites will compare.

findings.quote: contains £3.5 million to facilitate the development of HRA sites at East Street and Warwick Road

findings.paper_title: Draft Housing Revenue and Capital Budget 2027/28 & App 1 and 2 Non key
findings.headline: Canterbury aims to keep an HRA working balance or surplus of at least £1.5 million, a target the paper says has proved "extremely difficult" to meet in recent years.
findings.detail: The council is not permitted to set a deficit budget that would leave it with no reserves. The paper states the £1.5 million working balance aim has proved extremely difficult in recent years, and the proposed budget is described as financially viable and legally compliant.
findings.matters: A minimum HRA working balance target that has been hard to hold is a reserve position that finance directors and lenders will test against the final budget.
findings.figures: at least £1.5 million working balance or surplus
findings.quote: aims to retain a prudent HRA working balance or surplus of at least £1.5 million, which has proved extremely difficult in recent years.

findings.headline: Some garage tenants have terminated their licences since the garage management change.
findings.detail: The paper says the management company has received no adverse feedback on the 2026/27 rent increase and that there is no evidence that garage costs or affordability were a factor. It reports a gradual and modest increase in overall garage occupancy.
findings.matters: Surrenders following an outsourcing handover affect the rental income the upgrade programme depends on, which is relevant to any council running a similar garage model.

findings.matters: The outsourced garage model ties capital upgrades to a rental income commitment, a structure other councils considering similar arrangements will compare.

findings.paper_title: Financial Outlook and draft budget 2027-28 NK
findings.headline: The forecast shows a budget gap in 2029/30, after the use of reserves, of just under £1m.
findings.detail: The paper says the forecast shows a budget gap in 2029/30, taking into account use of reserves, of just under £1m. It calls this an estimate based on future spending plans and assumptions.
findings.matters: A medium-term gap that is still open means savings must be found or reserves used, which finance directors and lenders track against the medium-term plan.
findings.figures: just under £1m budget gap in 2029/30
findings.quote: Looking beyond 2027/28, the forecast shows a budget gap, taking into consideration the use of reserves, of just under £1m in 2029/30.

findings.paper_title: Financial Outlook and draft budget 2027-28 NK
findings.headline: The Kent Superannuation Scheme backfunding contribution has decreased as the fund becomes near fully funded for the council.
findings.detail: The paper says the triennial review in 2026/27 reduced the ongoing contribution rate, and the reduction is included in the budget. It says backfunding was reduced because the council's share of the fund is near fully funded.
findings.matters: A reduction in pension backfunding frees budget capacity and signals a funding position that finance directors across the Kent scheme will be comparing.
findings.quote: A decrease in backfunding contributions was agreed as the fund becomes near fully funded for the council and the reduction has been included in the budget.

findings.paper_title: Financial Outlook and draft budget 2027-28 NK
findings.headline: The draft budget assumes a 2.97% council tax increase, equal to £7.56 a year for a band D property.
findings.detail: The paper proposes a 2.97% increase, under the 3% limit assumed for 2027/28. It rejects a freeze, which it says would need £459,000 of additional ongoing savings or income.
findings.matters: Council tax is the largest income line in the draft budget, and the assumed increase sits close to the referendum limit that peers face.
findings.figures: 2.97% council tax increase; £7.56 a year for a band D property; £459,000 consequence of a freeze
findings.quote: a council tax increase of 2.97% (£7.56 a year for a band D property)

findings.paper_title: Financial Outlook and draft budget 2027-28 NK
findings.headline: Canterbury will not join the Kent business rates pool for 2027/28.
findings.detail: The paper says the council is not currently in the Kent Pool and will not join for 2027/28, because the risks to the pool outweigh the potential benefits. Under pooling, councils share growth but cover reductions up to a joint safety net.
findings.matters: Pooling decisions change how business rates risk and growth are shared, which finance officers at other Kent councils will be weighing too.
findings.quote: The council is not currently in the Kent Pool and will not be part of it for 2027/28, as the risks to the pool of Canterbury’s membership outweigh the potential benefits.

findings.paper_title: Financial Outlook and draft budget 2027-28 NK
findings.headline: The council's draft capital programme includes a £10m provision for possible additional parking capacity at Wincheap Park and Ride, subject to a decision and business case.
findings.detail: The paper says the £10m is phased as £0.5m in 2026/27, £1.5m in 2027/28 and £8m in 2028/29. Delivery depends on a future Council decision and an approved business case.
findings.matters: A large capital provision contingent on a future decision and business case is a commitment a lender or finance director would want to track against borrowing.
findings.quote: The programme continues to include a total provision of £10m across 2026/27 to 2028/29 to assess and, subject to a future Council decision and an approved business case

findings.paper_title: Financial Outlook and draft budget 2027-28 NK
findings.headline: General Fund total financing costs are budgeted at £13.2m in 2026/27, rising to £13.3m by the end of 2027/28.
findings.detail: The paper says these costs include MRP and interest for owned and leased assets and equal 12.7% of gross expenditure. It says the level of borrowing increases the risk that falling income could force reductions in services to meet borrowing costs.
findings.matters: Financing costs as a share of gross expenditure are a standard test of borrowing exposure for both finance directors and lenders.
findings.figures: £13.2m financing costs in 2026/27; £13.3m by end of 2027/28; 12.7% of gross expenditure
findings.quote: In 2026/27, the General Fund total financing costs are budgeted at £13.2m

findings.paper_title: Financial Outlook and draft budget 2027-28 NK
findings.headline: Estimated additional inflation impact on General Fund revenues in 2027/28 is £1.9m.
findings.detail: The paper estimates direct and indirect inflation will add £1.9m to General Fund revenue costs in 2027/28. It also says that if the position is worse in January, additional savings may need to be considered.
findings.matters: Inflation cost pressures of this size against a reserve-funded gap are the pressure other councils are describing, and the paper ties it to possible additional savings.
findings.figures: £1.9m additional inflation impact in 2027/28
findings.quote: It is currently estimated the impact of the increase of direct and indirect inflation will be an additional £1.9m to the General Fund’s revenues in 2027/28.

findings.paper_title: Financial Outlook and draft budget 2027-28 NK
findings.headline: The current 2026/27 budget did not require the use of reserves to balance.
findings.detail: The paper states that the 2026/27 budget was balanced without drawing on reserves. The reserve draw is forecast only from 2027/28.
findings.matters: A finance director at another council will note that the current year balances without a reserve draw, which is a change from the reserve-supported position the paper describes for the following year.
findings.quote: The current year’s budget did not require the use of reserves in 2026/27 to balance the budget.

findings.paper_title: Financial Outlook and draft budget 2027-28 NK
findings.headline: The paper states that annual contributions to reserves are required to rebuild reserve levels but are not possible under the current budget assumptions.
findings.detail: The paper says the council's reserves have been depleted over recent years and that it will need to reinvest to rebuild them. It sets out an aim to rebuild reserves and reduce budget risk rather than increase it.
findings.matters: Peers and lenders assess resilience by whether a council can rebuild reserves, and this paper says it cannot under current assumptions.
findings.quote: Annual contributions to reserves are required to rebuild reserve levels, but this is not possible with the current budget assumptions.

findings.paper_title: Financial Outlook and draft budget 2027-28 NK
findings.headline: The draft 2027/28 budget has a £0.4m gap, which the council proposes to bridge from the budget stabilisation reserve.
findings.detail: The paper estimates a 2027/28 budget gap of £0.4m and proposes using the budget stabilisation reserve to close it. The paper says it will need to plan to rebuild reserves and reduce the level of risk in its budget.
findings.matters: A finance director, or a lender, will want to see a reserve being drawn to balance the budget, and the paper states the council's reserves are reduced.
findings.figures: £0.4m budget gap in 2027/28; £0.4m budget stabilisation reserve use
findings.quote: in 2027/28 it is estimated that there will be a budget gap of £0.4m. It is proposed to utilise the budget stabilisation reserve to bridge the gap.

findings.headline: Asbestos removal is forecast at £100,000 for 2026/27, against an original budget of £222,990.
findings.detail: Asbestos removal spend was £10,554 in 2025/26. The 2026/27 original budget is £222,990, and the forecast is £100,000, with £229,680 estimated for 2027/28.
findings.matters: The gap between the original budget and the forecast, against very low prior-year spend, shows how budget-setting assumptions can diverge from actual activity.

findings.headline: Total planned maintenance is forecast at £1,855,401 for 2026/27, against an original budget of £2,268,850.
findings.detail: Planned maintenance spend was £1,475,457 in 2025/26. The 2026/27 original budget is £2,268,850 and the forecast is £1,855,401, with £2,514,942 estimated for 2027/28.
findings.matters: A forecast well below the original planned maintenance budget would show whether planned work is being delivered as scheduled or deferred, which bears on future capital and revenue pressure.

findings.headline: The Housing Repairs Account is forecast at £9,271,573 for 2026/27, against an original budget of £9,565,643.
findings.detail: The total account forecast sits below the original 2026/27 budget. The 2027/28 estimate is £11,119,736, which is higher than the 2026/27 original budget.
findings.matters: Comparing forecast with original budget for the whole account shows whether the council is on track to spend within its housing repairs envelope, and the 2027/28 step-up shows the size of the next year's ask.
findings.quote: Total housing repairs account 9,565,643 9,271,573 11,119,736

findings.headline: Voids are forecast at £1,508,000 for 2026/27, against an original budget of £1,008,000.
findings.detail: The paper's table shows voids spend of £2,616,763 in 2025/26, an original 2026/27 budget of £1,008,000 and a 2026/27 forecast of £1,508,000. The 2027/28 estimate is £1,738,240.
findings.matters: A finance director would want to know whether the void budget was set too low against the spend the council has actually been running, since the forecast is already above it.

findings.headline: Taxi and private hire fees are marked as subject to separate consultation, with the taxi vehicle initial fee shown at £466.96 in both 2026/27 and 2027/28
findings.detail: The taxi and private hire section carries a note that its fees are subject to separate consultation. The schedule shows most initial and renewal fees at 0% change for 2027/28, and the paper does not say whether the schedule will change after that consultation.
findings.matters: A licensing fee schedule held pending consultation means the income from these fees for 2027/28 depends on an outcome the paper does not yet give, which a finance officer would need to reflect in the budget.
findings.figures: Taxi vehicle initial £466.96 (2026/27) and £466.96 (2027/28), 0%; Private Hire vehicle initial £347.83 in both years, 0%
findings.quote: Taxi and Private Hire Subject to seperate consulation

findings.headline: Defra-set statutory pollution prevention permit fees for 2027/28 are shown as TBC, with the 2026/27 standard process application fee at £1,650.00
findings.detail: The schedule lists pollution prevention permit fees with the 2026/27 charge filled in and the 2027/28 charge marked TBC against Defra. The council cannot set these fees itself, so the income for 2027/28 is not yet known.
findings.matters: Statutory fees set by central government and not yet published leave a gap in forecast income for any council that delivers this regulatory function, and an unknown amount for the budget.
findings.figures: Standard process application £1,650.00 (2026/27); Substantial change, standard process £1,050.00 (2026/27); 2027/28 charges shown as TBC
findings.quote: Standard process application 1,650.00 TBC Defra No

findings.headline: Council tax summons fee is proposed to fall from £82.16 to £60.00 and the liability fee from £62.40 to £40.00 from 01/04/2027
findings.detail: The schedule shows the council tax summons charge reducing by 27% and the council tax liability charge by 36%, with the same reductions proposed for the NDR summons and liability charges. The paper does not state the reason for the change.
findings.matters: Summons and liability charges are cost-recovery income on council tax and business rates enforcement, so a finance director would want to know how far a fall of this size reduces recovery income and whether it changes the cost of collection.
findings.figures: Council tax summons £82.16 to £60.00 (-27%); council tax liability £62.40 to £40.00 (-36%); NDR summons £82.16 to £60.00 (-27%); NDR liability £62.40 to £40.00 (-36%)
findings.quote: Council tax summons 82.16 60.00

findings.paper_title: Appendix D - Estimated effect of 4.5% rent increase
findings.headline: Canterbury estimates average 2027/28 social rents of £99.42 (studio) to £174.74 (5-bed) per week, after a 4.5% increase and £1 rent convergence.
findings.detail: The appendix applies CPI+1% (4.5%) and £1 of rent convergence to 2026/27 average social rents for each property size. It also shows affordable rent estimates for 1-bed to 5-bed properties, which rise to £150.05 to £328.90 per week.
findings.matters: Rent income is a core part of the housing revenue account, and a finance officer at another council can compare this rent-setting basis against their own 2027/28 assumptions.

findings.quote: Estimated effect of 4.5% rent increase and rent convergence on average weekly rents over 50 weeks in 2027/28

findings.paper_title: Appendix B - HRA Capital Programme and Financing
findings.headline: Grants for 2026/27 are forecast at £6,108,862, against an original estimate of £2,200,000.
findings.detail: The original 2026/27 estimate for grants is £2,200,000. The current estimate and the forecast are both £6,108,862. The estimate for 2027/28 falls to £3,581,282.
findings.matters: Grant funding that is nearly three times the original estimate reduces the council's reliance on borrowing and reserves for the 2026/27 programme.
findings.figures: £2,200,000 (2026/27 original); £6,108,862 (2026/27 current estimate and forecast); £3,581,282 (2027/28 estimate)

findings.paper_title: Appendix B - HRA Capital Programme and Financing
findings.headline: Forecast 2026/27 1-4-1 capital receipts are £566,880, against a current estimate of £2,709,365.
findings.detail: The current estimate for 2026/27 includes £2,709,365 of 1-4-1 capital receipts. The forecast is £566,880. The paper does not give a reason for the change.
findings.matters: 1-4-1 receipts fund a share of replacement housing, so a forecast well below the current estimate affects how much of the new-build programme can be financed without borrowing or grant.

findings.paper_title: Appendix B - HRA Capital Programme and Financing
findings.headline: Energy saving measures are estimated at £6,837,000 for 2026/27, up from an original £3,750,000.
findings.detail: The current 2026/27 estimate for energy saving measures is £6,837,000, against an original £3,750,000. The forecast is £6,806,844, which is £30,156 below the current estimate. The estimate for 2027/28 is £5,303,202.
findings.matters: A large rise in energy-efficiency spend on HRA stock is a material call on capital resources, and other councils planning retrofit programmes would want to compare the scale.

findings.paper_title: Appendix B - HRA Capital Programme and Financing
findings.headline: Housing development schemes are forecast at £2,857,515 for 2026/27, against a current estimate of £5,000,000.
findings.detail: The current 2026/27 estimate for housing development schemes is £5,000,000, the same as the original. The forecast is £2,857,515, which is £2,142,485 lower. The estimate for 2027/28 is £3,536,763.
findings.matters: A new-build programme forecast well below its current estimate shows delivery running behind the budget, which bears on the pace of the council's new housing supply.
findings.figures: £5,000,000 (2026/27 original and current estimate); £2,857,515 (2026/27 forecast); £3,536,763 (2027/28 estimate)

findings.paper_title: Appendix B - HRA Capital Programme and Financing
findings.headline: Forecast 2026/27 HRA capital expenditure is £17,344,259, against a current estimate of £19,417,000.
findings.detail: The forecast for 2026/27 total capital expenditure is £2,072,741 below the current estimate. The original estimate was £15,980,000. Forecast expenditure for 2027/28 is £21,623,985.
findings.matters: A forecast below the current estimate shows the programme is running behind its approved budget, which affects planned financing and borrowing decisions.

findings.paper_title: Appendix B - HRA Capital Programme and Financing
findings.headline: External borrowing of £9,030,000 in the original 2026/27 budget is £0 in the current and forecast 2026/27 figures.
findings.detail: The original 2026/27 financing includes £9,030,000 of external borrowing. The current estimate and the forecast both show nil external borrowing for 2026/27 and for each year to 2031/32. The paper does not state the reason for the change.
findings.matters: A finance director at another council, or a lender, would want to know that a planned £9,030,000 borrowing requirement for HRA capital has been removed from the 2026/27 financing.
findings.figures: £9,030,000 (original 2026/27 external borrowing); £0 (current and forecast 2026/27 external borrowing)
findings.quote: 0 External borrowing 9,030,000 0 0 0 0 0 0 0

findings.headline: Stage 1 complaints completed on time at 65.06% against 90% target; Stage 2 at 82% against 90% target
findings.detail: Complaint handling performance remains below target. Stage 1 complaints are completed on time in 65.06% of cases (target 90%), and Stage 2 in 82% of cases (target 90%). The council reports significant improvement compared to the prior year, with reduced response times and a new CRM system introduced in the latter stages of the year.
findings.matters: Complaint handling indicates management capacity and service quality. While below-target performance could suggest resource or process issues, the positive trend and system improvements indicate management action and suggest this is being actively addressed.
findings.figures: Stage 1: 65.06% vs 90% target (25-point gap); Stage 2: 82% vs 90% target (8-point gap)
findings.quote: % of stage 1 complaints completed on time 65.06%Target: 90%

findings.headline: Residential rent arrears at 3.51% of annual income, below 4.55% target; former tenant arrears reduced to £950K
findings.detail: The Income Recovery dashboard shows current residential rent arrears at 3.51% of projected annual income, below the 4.55% target. Former tenant arrears have reduced from £1.1M to £0.95M following introduction of dedicated recovery resources in January 2026. The council wrote off £260K during the year, including £220K in statute-barred debt.
findings.matters: Rent collection performance is fundamental to HRA financial viability and the council's capacity to service debt. Strong collection performance particularly during welfare system transition demonstrates effective income recovery management and control over the primary revenue stream.
findings.figures: Current arrears: 3.51% vs 4.55% target; Current value: £1.11M; Former tenant arrears: £0.95M (down from £1.1M); Debt written off: £0.26M
findings.quote: The Income Recovery team has exceeded their target by keeping current rent arrears at 3.51%, well below the 4.55% KPI. This is a strong result given the continued transition from Housing Benefit to Universal Credit, which can initially place tenants into arrears.

findings.headline: 279 dwellings with overdue electrical installation condition reports; domestic EICR compliance at 94.37% against 100% target
findings.detail: Domestic EICR (electrical installation condition report) compliance stands at 94.37% against a 100% target, representing 279 dwellings with overdue inspections. The council has implemented a new door-knocking process to gain access to older properties. Compliance has been increasing slowly.
findings.matters: Electrical safety certification is a legal compliance requirement. A backlog of 279 overdue inspections represents both safety risks to tenants and potential legal and reputational exposure. It may also indicate asset management or operational capacity issues.
findings.figures: Overdue EICRs: 279 dwellings; Compliance: 94.37%; Target: 100%
findings.quote: we still have 279 dwellings with an overdue EICR, we have put a new door knocking process into place to try and help gain access to some of the oldest overdue properties

findings.headline: Sureserve gas repairs contractor underperforming: emergency repairs 87.83% on time against 98% target
findings.detail: Sureserve's performance on gas repairs is below target across multiple KPIs: emergency repairs at 87.83% on time (target 98%), urgent repairs at 92.57% (target 98%), and routine repairs at 91.72% (target 100%). The council commentary notes the contractor faced challenges from a Swale Heating acquisition and restructuring, and an action plan has been implemented.
findings.matters: Emergency repair underperformance raises safety concerns and impacts tenant satisfaction. Contractor underperformance indicates the council may face service delivery issues or need to enforce contractual terms, raising questions about contract management effectiveness and value for money.
findings.figures: Emergency repairs: 87.83% vs 98% target; Urgent repairs: 92.57% vs 98% target; Routine repairs: 91.72% vs 100% target
findings.quote: Their KPIs and contractual performance has not been where we would like them to be during 25/26 and we have worked with them on an action plan to address these issues.

findings.headline: Contractual invoices paid on time at 72.38% against 99% target
findings.detail: The Capital Spend dashboard shows that only 72.38% of contractual invoices are being paid on time, significantly below the 99% target. This represents a substantial gap in a key financial control metric.
findings.matters: Late invoice payment can indicate cash flow problems, administrative failures, or control weaknesses. It damages supplier relationships, may increase costs, and suggests the governance or administration issues that external lenders and auditors view as early-stage warning signs.
findings.figures: 72.38% on time; Target: 99%; Gap: 26.62 percentage points
findings.quote: % of contractual invoices paid on time 72.38%Target: 99%

findings.headline: Estimated rental income loss of £804.95K due to void properties taking average 141.76 days to relet
findings.detail: The Voids All Relets dashboard shows average relet time of 141.76 days across all void categories (major work 138.73 days, minor work 102.93 days). With 230 terminations in the year, this extended void period is estimated to have generated rental income loss of £804.95K and service charge loss of £54.28K.
findings.matters: Extended void periods directly reduce HRA rental income, affecting cash available for service maintenance and debt service. A lender would want to understand whether this is a systemic issue, what is causing delays, and whether the council has action plans to reduce relet times.
findings.figures: Average relet days: 141.76; Major work: 138.73 days; Minor work: 102.93 days; Income loss: £804.95K; Service charge loss: £54.28K; Total terminations: 230; Total relets: 338
findings.quote: Estimated loss of rental income £804.95K

findings.headline: Sureserve repairs contractor missed emergency, urgent and routine repair targets following Swale Heating acquisition; action plan in place
findings.detail: Major repairs contractor Sureserve underperformed across all KPI categories in 2025-26: emergency 87.83% vs 98% target (397 of 452); urgent 92.57% vs 98% (1,521 of 1,643); routine 91.72% vs 100% (1,473 of 1,603); appointment keeping 91.15% vs 98% (3,757 of 4,122); single-visit completion 83.67% vs 85%. Underperformance followed Swale Heating acquisition and organizational restructuring. Council reports positive engagement from Sureserve and action plan in place with progress described as quick and in line with improvement plans.
findings.matters: Major contractor underperformance affects service quality and tenant satisfaction, which drive arrears and voids; outcome of remediation plan will determine whether additional investment or contract remedies required
findings.figures: Emergency 87.83% vs 98% target; urgent 92.57% vs 98%; routine 91.72% vs 100%; appointments 91.15% vs 98%; single visit 83.67% vs 85%
findings.quote: Sureserve have had a difficult year having acquired Swale Heating, they have centralised their resources and rebuilt a significant internal delivery process. Their KPIs and contractual performance has not been where we would like them to be during 2025-26, and we have worked with them on an action plan to address these issues.

findings.headline: Former tenant arrears reduced by £150,000 to £0.95m following targeted income recovery resource addition in January 2026
findings.detail: Resource was added to income recovery team from January 2026 specifically for former tenant arrears. This resulted in reduction from £1.1m to £0.95m in the following quarter. Historic write-offs applied where relevant; processes audited; direct income being received. Shows targeted financial investment generating measurable return.
findings.matters: Demonstrates proactive debt management and financial discipline; targeted resource investment is generating cash recovery (£150k in single quarter) with clear ROI, relevant to HRA budget planning
findings.figures: Former tenant arrears £1.1m to £0.95m; £150,000 reduction; resource added January 2026
findings.quote: Resource was added to the income recovery team to focus on Former Tenant Arrear from January 2026. This resulted in a marked reduction in Former Tenant Arrears from £1.1m to £0.95m in that quarter.

findings.headline: Current tenant arrears 3.53% of rental income, well within 4.55% target despite Universal Credit migration from Housing Benefit
findings.detail: Current residential arrears at end March 2026 were 3.53% of total expected annual rental income, comfortably within 4.55% target. Income recovery team has driven reduction despite ongoing benefits system migration from Housing Benefit to Universal Credit. Council notes target is higher than neighbouring local authorities and will review KPI for next reporting period following East Kent Partnership Audit findings.
findings.matters: Rent arrears management is central to HRA revenue sustainability; maintaining below-target arrears amid major welfare system transition demonstrates effective financial management and reduces bad debt risk
findings.figures: 3.53% current arrears against <4.55% target
findings.quote: The target for current residential arrears is <4.55% and performance is well within the current target at 3.53% of total expected annual rental income. The income recovery team have worked hard to drive this reduction in percentage of arrears compared to Q1 against a backdrop of challenges within the benefits system of migration of Housing Benefit to Universal Credit.

findings.headline: Building Safety Regulator: Elizabeth Court has three compliance notices, evidence deadline July 2026; Windsor House remedial works started April, completion May 2027
findings.detail: Elizabeth Court safety case submission resulted in three compliance notices. Council given until July 2026 to submit evidence; some submitted with remainder pending external compartmentation survey due June. Windsor House remedial works approved by Building Safety Regulator 30 April 2026 and commenced. Scaffolding erection 12-16 weeks, cladding removal late July/early August targeted, project completion early May 2027. Works include roof repairs and water tank replacement.
findings.matters: High-rise building safety is regulatory priority; compliance failures could affect regulatory standing; timelines consume capital resources over next 12 months and affect housing stock availability and HRA debt service capacity
findings.figures: Elizabeth Court deadline July 2026; Windsor House scaffolding 12-16 weeks; cladding removal late July/August; completion May 2027
findings.quote: Following the submission of the building safety case for Elizabeth Court, 3 compliance notices were issued to the council setting out what was required to comply and ensure the safety case was approved. We have been given until July to submit the evidence. The remedial works to Windsor House have now started following approval by the Building Safety Regulator on 30 April this year.

findings.headline: Capital maintenance programme 39% underspent: £3.9m of £10m budget unspent, driven by retrofit delay and building safety approval timings
findings.detail: Capital budget of £10,015,000 resulted in spend of £6,071,895 at end March 2026. Main underspend drivers: retrofit programme to c800 homes started later than planned due to contractor issues (phase 1 of c80 homes underway); fire safety works at Windsor House delayed pending Building Safety Regulator approval (received April); garage improvements not yet invoiced. Match funding for £6.6m retrofit grant being rolled to future years.
findings.matters: Material capital programme underspend affects HRA cash flow timing and borrowing requirement; retrofit delay affects drawdown of £6.6m grant funding; signals delivery and contractor management challenges
findings.figures: £10,015,000 budget; £6,071,895 spend; £3.9m underspend (39.4%); £6.6m retrofit grant fund; c800 homes target retrofit
findings.quote: The capital programme for building maintenance had a budget of £10,015,000. The total spend at end of March 2026 was £6,071,895. The delays to the fire safety works at Windsor House (approval was eventually given to proceed in April this year), garage improvement works which are underway but will be completed and invoiced in the next financial year and the retrofit project.

findings.headline: Sureserve contractor issues represent largest single complaint theme at 16.03% of Stage 1 complaints
findings.detail: Contractor-Sureserve accounts for 16.03% of all Stage 1 complaints, the single most common theme. A performance improvement plan was agreed with the heating contractor to address repeated cancellations, with the council working to reduce rescheduling frequency.
findings.matters: High contractor complaint rate indicates contract performance issues or procurement management considerations that may affect service delivery and resident satisfaction.
findings.figures: 16.03% of Stage 1 complaints; repairs-related issues (Repairs Needed and Repairs Outstanding combined) account for approximately 19% of complaints
findings.quote: The most prominent theme is contractor - Sureserve, accounting for 16.03% of all Stage 1 complaints, followed by repairs needed at 11.95%.

findings.headline: Complaint intake increased significantly year-on-year despite closure rate improvements
findings.detail: The council closed 157.3% more Stage 1 complaints on time and 228% more Stage 2 complaints on time compared to the prior year, but this occurred 'despite seeing significant rises in complaint intake across our housing service'.
findings.matters: Rising complaint volumes indicate either increased service problems or heightened resident awareness, both signalling demand pressure that may require continued resource commitment.
findings.figures: 157.3% increase in Stage 1 complaints closed on time; 228% increase in Stage 2 complaints closed on time; complaint intake volumes described as 'significant rises'
findings.quote: We closed 157.3% more stage 1 complaints on time this year compared to the previous year, and 228% more stage 2 complaints on time, despite seeing significant rises in complaint intake across our housing service.

findings.headline: New CRM system implementation associated with measurable improvement in complaint handling performance
findings.detail: March 2026 achieved the highest Stage 1 performance of the year at 80% with fewer late closures. This performance was explicitly linked to implementation of a new CRM system and heightened visibility of complaint workflows for responding officers.
findings.matters: System investment yielded documented performance gains, demonstrating a measurable return on technology investment.
findings.figures: 80% performance in March; previous quarterly average 65.06%
findings.quote: This quarter's strong performance is linked to the implementation of a new CRM system and heightened visibility of complaint workflows for responding officers.

findings.headline: Council created two new Neighbourhood Management Assistant posts to address complaint-related staffing gaps
findings.detail: Complaints relating to delayed or absent responses from officers prompted creation of two Neighbourhood Management Assistant posts aimed at improving responsiveness and communication with residents. Officers were also required to prioritise resident contact by dedicating the first and last hour of each working day to responding to tenant enquiries.
findings.matters: New recurring staffing costs represent a direct financial commitment to address service delivery shortfalls in complaint handling.
findings.figures: Two new posts created
findings.quote: Complaints relating to delayed or absent responses from officers were used to support the creation of two Neighbourhood Management Assistant posts, aimed at improving responsiveness and communication with residents.

findings.headline: Councillor enquiries averaged 7.4 days to close against internal target of 3 days
findings.detail: Councillor enquiries took 7.4 days on average to close while targeting 3 days, though MP enquiries (7.6 days) met their 10-day target. The data is reported for enquiries received through the Service Issues mailbox.
findings.matters: Missed councillor enquiry targets indicate political pressure and resource constraints in responsive services.
findings.figures: 7.4 days average vs 3 day target for councillor enquiries; 7.6 days vs 10 working days for MP enquiries
findings.quote: It has taken on average 7.4 days to close a Cllr enquiry with an in-house target of 3, and 7.6 days to close an MP enquiry with an in-house target of 10 working days.

findings.headline: Stage 1 housing complaints closed at 65.06% within timescales against 90% performance target for 2025-26
findings.detail: 352 Stage 1 complaints were closed with 65.06% meeting timescales. Reactive Repairs (185 cases, 67.03% performance) and Neighbourhood Management were the main drivers of underperformance. Performance improved through the year, reaching 80% in March and 83.33% in Q4, but remained below target on average.
findings.matters: Sustained underperformance against internal service targets indicates either resource constraints or process issues in a high-volume service area.
findings.figures: 65.06% actual vs 90% target; 352 Stage 1 complaints closed; Reactive Repairs 185 cases at 67.03%; March reached 80%; Q4 Reactive Repairs achieved 83.33%
findings.quote: Across the year, a total of 352 Stage 1 complaints were closed, with an overall performance of 65.06% closed within timescales... overall performance remained below the 90% target.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 5 - Housing Ombudsman Complaints Handling Code Self-Assessment
findings.headline: Council acknowledges complaints were historically not always completed within statutory timescales; staff sent reminders and extensions now used appropriately
findings.detail: The council acknowledged in sections 6.3, 6.4 and 6.15 that stage 1 and stage 2 complaints were not historically completed within statutory timescales. Staff were sent reminders and provided support. The council states extensions are now being used appropriately, though it will continue to monitor compliance. The issue appeared to require multiple interventions to embed compliance.
findings.matters: A lender assesses whether operational controls and compliance frameworks are embedded in culture or require repeated enforcement; governance maturity is indicated by whether failures trigger system redesign rather than repeated staff reminders.
findings.figures: Historical: not all stage 1 complaints within 10 working days; not all stage 2 within 20 working days
findings.quote: We acknowledge this has not always happened and reminders have been sent to staff and they are being supported with this. More recently extensions are being used appropriately, but we will keep this under review.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 5 - Housing Ombudsman Complaints Handling Code Self-Assessment
findings.headline: Stage 1 complaints received doubled year-on-year and stage 2 complaints rose 129.5%, while on-time response performance increased 157% and 228% respectively.
findings.detail: Stage 1 complaints received doubled in 2025-26, but the council closed 157.3% more stage 1 complaints within the 10-working-day target. Stage 2 complaints increased by 129.5%, with 228% more closed on time within the 20-working-day target. The council states that high complaint volumes may indicate an accessible and well-publicised process, but does not analyse the underlying causes of the surge.
findings.matters: A peer finance director or lender needs to understand whether the complaint volume increase reflects deteriorating service quality or improved accessibility; sustained complaint surges can indicate systemic service issues or resource pressures in housing operations.
findings.figures: Stage 1 volume doubled; on-time closures increased 157.3%; stage 2 volume increased 129.5%; stage 2 on-time closures increased 228%
findings.quote: We closed 157.3% more stage 1 complaints on time during 2025-26 compared to the previous year, despite receiving double the amount of stage 1 complaints.

findings.headline: Council has committed £20m to Levelling Up Fund capital projects currently in progress.
findings.detail: Large capital enhancement projects are underway, described as delivering over £20m in public realm and historic environment improvements. These projects are intended to leave a legacy following the Local Government Reorganisation.
findings.matters: Large capital commitments carry delivery and financial risk. A lender assesses capital strategy, project delivery track record, and funding sources.
findings.figures: £20m total Levelling Up Fund projects
findings.quote: Several large projects are in progress, including the Levelling Up Fund projects, delivering over £20m of enhancements to the public realm and historic elements of Canterbury that will leave a legacy post-reorganisation.

findings.headline: Cyber incident is identified as one of the three highest-scoring risks on the Strategic Risk Register.
findings.detail: Cyber resilience is explicitly noted as a priority focus area. Cyber incident features alongside LGR and external relationships as top-tier risks, indicating material concern about digital security and potential operational/financial impact.
findings.matters: Cyber incidents can result in direct financial loss, service disruption, or compliance breaches. Identification as highest risk suggests material vulnerability exposure.
findings.figures: Risk score range: 20 down to 9; cyber listed among highest scoring risks
findings.quote: The highest risk scores were concerned with: • Local Government Reorganisation • Relationships with Trusts and other outside bodies • Cyber incident

findings.headline: Housing function underwent external governance review by the Housing Regulatory Inspector with formal action plan oversight.
findings.detail: The council has formally engaged with an external regulatory inspector on its housing function and is delivering a corrective action plan overseen by a dedicated Cabinet Committee. This indicates identified governance or service delivery issues in housing that require structured remediation.
findings.matters: Housing is typically a material financial function for councils. External governance review signals control weaknesses or service problems that could affect financial outcomes or compliance.
findings.figures: Not specified in this document
findings.quote: The housing function was recently reviewed by the Housing Regulatory Inspector. Delivery of the action plan arising from the review is being overseen by a Cabinet Committee.

findings.paper_title: 2025-26 TM outturn report draft (2)_Oksana Ivanova MT
findings.headline: Council breached treasury investment limit on unsecured funds, reaching £7.18m against £5m policy ceiling
findings.detail: During 2025-26, unsecured building society investments reached £7.18m, exceeding the council's £5m policy limit. The council states the breach lasted 'one night only' due to timing of fund arrivals, and was corrected the next day. However, the council frames the £5m limit as guidance rather than binding policy, treating the exceedance as a minor administrative lapse rather than a control failure.
findings.matters: A treasury control allowing deviation from stated investment limits—even if brief—suggests the operational framework does not reliably enforce its own risk thresholds; this is relevant to assessing whether the council's treasury function can be relied upon
findings.figures: Maximum during year £7.18m; limit £5m; difference £2.18m
findings.quote: The balance went above this level for one night only, because funds arrived in the account after the cut off time for placing them into more secure investments fund. The £7m was moved out the very next day into higher security deposit funds, so the position was quickly adjusted.

findings.paper_title: 2025-26 TM outturn report draft (2)_Oksana Ivanova MT
findings.headline: Whitefriars Development Unit Trust investment of £79.2m generated £5.2m income in 2025-26, below pre-pandemic levels due to retail sector pressures
findings.detail: Canterbury holds a strategic £79.2m investment in the Whitefriars Development Unit Trust. The investment generated £5.2m income in 2025-26, but this remains materially below pre-pandemic levels. The council attributes this to documented structural headwinds in retail: declining high street rents, online competition, and economic uncertainty affecting rent reviews. While low vacancy rates are maintained, income sustainability from this material asset concentration remains constrained.
findings.matters: A £79.2m retail asset in structural decline is a significant income risk; underperformance relative to historical norms suggests the valuation and future income projections may not be resilient to further sector deterioration
findings.figures: £79.2 million investment; £5.2 million income 2025-26; income below pre-pandemic levels
findings.quote: This strategic non-treasury investment generated £5.2 million of income in 2025-26. Income levels remain below those achieved prior to the pandemic, reflecting ongoing pressures within the retail sector. Nationally, high street retail rents have declined due to changing consumer behaviour, increased online competition, and continued economic uncertainty.

findings.headline: General Fund budget balanced through use of budgeted reserve drawdown of £0.4m with minimal surplus
findings.detail: The General Fund achieved only a £16,000 underspend for the year. The council had budgeted to draw £0.4m from its Budget Stabilisation reserve to balance the budget, and this occurred as planned. The Budget Stabilisation reserve ended the year at £3.4m after transfers to support other reserves and the General Fund Reserve.
findings.matters: Continued reliance on planned reserve drawdown to balance the in-year budget indicates structural revenue pressures and limited headroom to absorb unexpected costs or demand increases.
findings.figures: General Fund underspend £16,000; £0.4m reserve contribution used as budgeted; Budget Stabilisation reserve £3.4m
findings.quote: At the budget-setting stage, it was estimated the use of reserves to balance the budget for 2025/26 would be £0.4m from the budget stabilisation reserve.

findings.headline: Off-street parking income fell short by £404,000 at four city centre car parks due to Local Urban Fund works
findings.detail: Off-street parking revenue underperformed budget by £404,000, driven by closures or reduced capacity at four named car parks (Longport, Pound Lane, St Radigunds, Castle Row) affected by Local Urban Fund regeneration works. While other car parks performed to expectations, the concentration of impact on these four sites created a material shortfall.
findings.matters: Material dependency on parking income means that temporary disruptions from major works create revenue volatility; ongoing regeneration projects could create recurring income pressure.
findings.figures: £404,000 off-street parking overspend; four car parks affected by LUF works
findings.quote: Off street parking is reporting an overspend of £404,000, mainly due to income targets not being achieved at four car parks affected by LUF works: Longport, Pound Lane, St Radigunds and Castle Row.

findings.headline: HRA void property costs escalated by £1,617,000 driven by poor condition of properties on return and tenant damage
findings.detail: Repairs and maintenance across the HRA overspent by £1,413,000, with void costs (preparing empty properties for reletting) alone overrunning by £1,617,000. The council attributes this to properties returning in poor condition requiring extensive clearance, garden works, and significant refurbishment, plus tenant-induced damage. Costs are under review but the council notes they will continue to require close monitoring.
findings.matters: Large, recurring void cost overruns suggest either capital maintenance backlog in the housing stock or underlying property condition issues, both of which indicate asset quality concerns and future expenditure pressures.
findings.figures: £1,617,000 void cost overspend; £1,413,000 total HRA repairs and maintenance overspend
findings.quote: Void costs continue to increase substantially with a £1,617,000 overspend. Costs are currently under review to understand the reasons behind this rise.

findings.headline: Housing Benefit overspend £831,000 due to subsidy rates not covering supported and temporary accommodation costs
findings.detail: Housing Benefit payments exceeded budget by £831,000 because the government subsidy (frozen at January 2021 Local Housing Allowance rates) does not cover actual costs for supported and temporary accommodation. The council explicitly states this is likely to continue as accommodation needs grow but subsidy rates do not.
findings.matters: A structural subsidy shortfall in a core service creates a recurring, unavoidable budget pressure that local savings cannot resolve and must be funded from the council's own resources.
findings.figures: £831,000 overspend; subsidy not covering full payments for supported accommodation and temporary accommodation
findings.quote: It is a challenge being faced by every council. Unfortunately, while the demand for supported and temporary accommodation increases, as do rents, we still only receive the subsidy amount based on the January 2021 LHA rates.

findings.headline: Interest and Financing Costs overspend £602,000 due to increased borrowing and higher interest rates
findings.detail: The council spent £602,000 more than budgeted on interest and financing costs driven by increased capital borrowing and elevated interest rates in 2025/26. This represents ongoing cost pressure as the council has expanded its debt portfolio into a higher rate environment.
findings.matters: Rising debt servicing costs reduce financial flexibility and absorb money that could fund services. With rates remaining elevated, this is a structural pressure rather than temporary volatility.
findings.figures: £602,000 overspend; increased borrowing to finance capital expenditure; higher interest rates during 2025/26
findings.quote: Interest and Financing Costs are £602,000 overspent due to increased borrowing to finance capital expenditure and higher interest rates during 2025/26.

findings.headline: HRA energy efficiency investment stalled with £3.1m slippage pending assessment completion
findings.detail: Energy Savings Measures programme shows £3.087m slippage into 2026/27 due to delays in receiving retrofit assessments. The Retrofit Core Project Team is now assessing implications for the current and projected position through to 2028/29 to reprofiled budgets.
findings.matters: Significant delay to HRA energy efficiency investment affects the council's ability to improve housing stock condition and manage compliance obligations. Reprofiling through 2028/29 extends council exposure to this programme risk.
findings.figures: £3.087m slippage; programme extends through 2028/29; £1.5m grant repayment within this programme
findings.quote: The total budget slippage into 2026/27 for Energy Savings Measures is £3.087m

findings.headline: General Fund capital programme underspent by £7.5m with carry-forward slippage across all service areas
findings.detail: General Fund capital budget of £14.3m produced outturn of £6.3m, with £7.5m carry-forward requested. Slippage spans Corporate Services (£1.8m), People Services (£0.9m), Place Services (£2.4m), and Strategy & Improvement (£2.4m including £1.8m Levelling Up Fund match funding).
findings.matters: Large-scale slippage across all service areas suggests systemic delivery capacity or planning constraints, indicating the council may struggle to execute capital projects within forecast timescales.
findings.figures: £14.337m budget; £6.293m outturn; £7.523m carry forward; £521k net underspend
findings.quote: The total requested carry forward for the General Fund is £7.523m net (after taking account of specific grants, e.g. Housing schemes funded by housing capital receipts, grants and loans).

findings.headline: Warm Homes Social Housing Fund project delayed, requiring £1.5m grant repayment
findings.detail: The Warm Homes Social Housing Fund Project experienced significant delays in receiving retrofit assessments and progressing to design stage. No installation works were carried out in 2025/26, making a £1.5m grant repayment necessary. Negotiations with DESNZ to descope the first phase have been approved, creating opportunity to claim further 2026/27 funding, but the decision date is pending.
findings.matters: A £1.5m grant repayment materially affects cash flow and indicates delivery failure on a government-funded programme. Future funding of £6.6m depends on a pending DESNZ decision, creating uncertainty over the council's ability to complete the retrofit programme.
findings.figures: £1.5m of £1.9m 2025/26 grant must be repaid; original £6.6m allocation; further 2026/27 funding claim pending
findings.quote: There were significant delays in receiving the required retrofit assessments and subsequently progressing these to the design stage. As a result, no installation works were carried out in 2025/26. The consequence of this delay is that £1.5m of the £1.9m grant allocated for 2025/26 will have to be repaid.

findings.headline: General Fund Reserve at minimum threshold with S151 officer emphasis on urgency
findings.detail: The General Fund Reserve is projected at £2m (1 April 2026) against a recommended minimum of £3m or 15% of net budget. The S151 officer explicitly advises that 'every effort must be made to achieve the agreed savings plan' and the council 'should avoid, at all costs' the reserve falling below 15%.
findings.matters: The reserve is at the minimum threshold with no buffer. The S151 officer's emphasis signals that any shortfall — from inflation, pay, or income risks already identified — will push the council below the safety level and force emergency action.
findings.figures: Estimated balance 1 April 2026: £2,000k; recommended minimum: £3m or 15% (net budget £25.84m = 15% = £3.88m)
findings.quote: The formal advice of the Section 151 officer to the council is every effort must be made to achieve the agreed savings plan in order to ensure financial sustainability and preserve the level of reserves for future commitments. The Council should avoid, at all costs, the General Fund Reserve balance reducing below 15% of its Net Service Expenditure.

findings.headline: Budget balanced in 2026/27 but requires £300k and then £1,150k savings in following two years
findings.detail: The 2026-27 budget is balanced, but the three-year plan requires no savings 2026/27, then £300k in 2027/28 and £1,150k in 2028/29. The S151 officer states the council can no longer 'continue with that approach' of maintaining service levels and councillors must make 'very difficult decisions'.
findings.matters: The current balance depends on delaying savings; the council is signalling that service cuts are inevitable in the medium term, creating uncertainty about the sustainability of service delivery to justify borrowing.
findings.quote: The council has a successful track record in achieving a balanced budget while maintaining service levels, however in the current situation it will be impossible to continue with that approach. Councillors will need to face some very difficult decisions over the next few years in order to have a sustainable financial position.

findings.headline: Homelessness and rough sleeping funding reduced by £1.2m through grant consolidation
findings.detail: Direct funding for homelessness, rough sleeping, domestic abuse and discretionary housing payments falls from £2.8m to £1.6m. While RSG uplift is expected to offset this, the structural shift concentrates these services into a consolidated funding stream without ringfencing.
findings.matters: A lender needs to know whether these services remain adequately funded under a new framework, and whether consolidation means funding shortfalls in one area will not be recoverable from the general fund.
findings.figures: Direct funding reduction from £2.8m to £1.6m
findings.quote: For 2026/27, the government has streamlined multiple service-specific grants into a single RSG. This consolidation includes previous allocations for homelessness, rough sleeping, domestic abuse and discretionary housing payments which now form part of the calculation for the council's CSP. As a result of this restructuring, direct funding for these services will reduce from £2.8 million to £1.6m.

findings.headline: Local Government Reorganisation will consume £500k annually from Budget Stabilisation Reserve
findings.detail: The council faces major structural reorganisation, with £500k allocated annually to LGR costs. This is described as requiring significant resource allocation, careful planning and robust governance. This drawdown reduces the reserve available to cover other risks.
findings.matters: LGR is a non-operational cost reducing available contingency. The timing and final costs are uncertain; £500k per year may prove insufficient if reorganisation requires more resource, further depleting reserves.
findings.figures: £500k allocated in 2025/26, further £500k each year
findings.quote: These changes will have significant strategic and operational implications for the council.
